models.name: Minutes of life expectancy lost per cigarette
models.estimates: Average loss of life expectancy attributable to each cigarette smoked, for people who keep smoking.

inputs.name: cigs_logged
inputs.how_we_get_it: sum of daily log over the period shown (day / week / month)

valid_for.population: Britain; mortality from British Doctors Study (men, to 2001) and Million Women Study (to 2011); consumption from 1996 UK survey
valid_for.exposure_range: assumes constant daily consumption over a smoking lifetime (15.8/day men, 13.6/day women in the calculation)

models.uncertainty: No confidence interval: this is an arithmetic scaling (11 min x 10/6.5 years lost, adjusted for cigarettes/day), not a fitted model. The authors say it is a population average across ages; per-person harm varies with puffing, inhalation, product and susceptibility, and may be somewhat high if toxicant per cigarette has fallen.

source.citation: Jackson SE, Jarvis MJ, West R. The price of a cigarette: 20 minutes of life? Addiction 2025;120(5):810-812
source.where: Article text, paragraph 3 (author accepted manuscript, p.2)
source.quote: this would lead to an increase in the estimated loss of life expectancy per cigarette to 20 minutes overall: 17 minutes for men (11*10/6.5) and 22 minutes for women ((11*11/6.5)*(15.8/13.6); see supplementary file for a more detailed explanation of the calculation).

supporting_sources.citation: Shaw M, Mitchell R, Dorling D. Time for a smoke? One cigarette reduces your life by 11 minutes. BMJ 2000;320:53
supporting_sources.note: Original 11-minute estimate, based on 6.5 years lost. NOT opened directly; value as described by Jackson 2025. Superseded by the 17/22 figures.

supporting_sources.citation: Doll R, Peto R, Boreham J, Sutherland I. Mortality in relation to smoking: 50 years' observations on male British doctors. BMJ 2004;328:1519
supporting_sources.note: Source of the ~10 years lost used in the 17-minute figure: 'Men born in 1900-1930 who smoked only cigarettes and continued smoking died on average about 10 years younger than lifelong non-smokers.'

models.caveats: Editorial-level calculation, UK data only. Harm is not linear per cigarette (see smoking-dose-chd), so do not present it as exact per-cigarette physics. Competing interests declared: RW is an unpaid advisor to the company making the Smoke Free app and paid advisor to an anti-smoking campaign agency; work commissioned by UK DHSC. It is peer-reviewed, not app marketing, but you may want to note this. Mirror use for quitting (minutes avoided per cigarette not smoked) belongs in H3.
models.user_copy: On average, each cigarette is linked to about 17–22 minutes of life expectancy lost. This is a population average, not a prediction for you.

models.name: Years of life lost, Indian smokers
models.estimates: Difference in median age at death between Indian smokers and similar non-smokers, and chance of dying between 30 and 70.

inputs.name: is_current_smoker
inputs.how_we_get_it: any cigarette/bidi logged in last 30 days

models.output_unit: years (median survival difference); % probability of death age 30–69

valid_for.population: India, nationally representative, deaths 2001–2003 (Million Death Study / RGI-CGHR)
valid_for.exposure_range: any smoking of bidis or cigarettes in the past 5 years; dose not used here

models.uncertainty: 99% CIs as printed. Case-control design with proxy (household) reporting of smoking and verbal-autopsy causes of death; controls unmatched. The 10-year cigarette figure is stated in the Discussion without a CI.

source.citation: Jha P, Jacob B, Gajalakshmi V, et al. A nationally representative case-control study of smoking and death in India. N Engl J Med 2008;358:1137-47
source.where: Results, 'Absolute risk' (p.1141) and Figure 3; cigarette 10-year figure in Discussion (p.1144)
source.quote: The median ages at death suggested that male smokers will die an average of approximately 6 years (99% CI, 5 to 7) earlier than their nonsmoking counterparts.

supporting_sources.citation: Doll R et al. BMJ 2004;328:1519 (British doctors, 50 years)
supporting_sources.note: UK continuing cigarette smokers died about 10 years younger; matches the Indian cigarette-only estimate.

models.caveats: Group averages, not personal life expectancy. Women's estimate rests on few smokers (about 5% of women smoked). Cigarette 10-year gap: quote is 'the hazard of cigarette smoking (risk ratio, 2.2) was even higher ... suggesting about a 10-year gap in median survival'. Do not show before the user has confirmed they smoke regularly.
models.user_copy: In Indian data, people who smoke die on average about 6–8 years earlier than people who don't (range 5–11 years); for cigarette smokers it was about 10 years.

valid_for.sex: men for the dose bands; both for any-smoking rows
valid_for.exposure_range: 1–7 and 8+ cigarettes/day; no finer bands in main text

source.where: Results, 'Relative risk in subgroups' (p.1141); any-smoking rows from Table 2
source.quote: among those who smoked only cigarettes (risk ratio for one to seven cigarettes per day, 1.8; risk ratio for eight or more, 2.9; P<0.001 for both trends)

supporting_sources.note: Norway, 1–4/day, all-cause death RR 1.57 (1.33–1.85) men, 1.47 (1.19–1.82) women.

models.uncertainty: No CIs printed in Table 3 (chi-square for trend 576). Death counts per cell given in brackets (403, 641, 577) indicate reasonable precision.

source.citation: Doll R, Peto R, Boreham J, Sutherland I. Mortality in relation to smoking: 50 years' observations on male British doctors. BMJ 2004;328:1519

models.caveats: Men only, highly educated, historical cigarettes. Use smoking-dose-allcause-india as the primary Indian estimate and this as the Western reference.
models.user_copy: Among older long-term smokers, the yearly risk of death was about 1.8 times a non-smoker's at under 15 a day and about 2.6 times at 25 or more.

inputs.name: cigs_per_day
inputs.how_we_get_it: daily log, 90-day average (to capture non-daily smoking)

valid_for.population: USA, NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study, baseline 2004–2005, follow-up to 2011

models.uncertainty: Only 159 people in the <1/day group (wide CI 1.07–2.51). Self-reported lifetime history. Adjusted for sex, race/ethnicity, education, physical activity, alcohol.

source.citation: Inoue-Choi M, Liao LM, Reyes-Guzman C, et al. Association of long-term, low-intensity smoking with all-cause and cause-specific mortality in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study. JAMA Intern Med 2017;177(1):87-95
source.quote: Relative to never smokers, consistent smokers of fewer than 1 CPD (HR, 1.64; 95% CI, 1.07–2.51) and 1 to 10 CPD (HR, 1.87; 95% CI, 1.64–2.13) had a higher all-cause mortality risk.

supporting_sources.citation: Bjartveit K, Tverdal A. Tob Control 2005;14:315-320
supporting_sources.note: 1–4/day all-cause death RR 1.57 (1.33–1.85) men, 1.47 (1.19–1.82) women; Norway, age 35–49 at entry, 1970s–2002. Abstract only.

models.caveats: Abstract text was read via the PMC abstract (search index); the full article was not fetched. Former-smoker quit-age rows at <50 are in the full text only. Best used to support the 'light smoking isn't safe' message rather than as a precise number.
models.user_copy: Even smoking under 1 cigarette a day over years was linked to about 1.6 times the risk of death (range 1.1–2.5); 1–10 a day, about 1.9 times.

models.name: Heart attack / coronary heart disease risk by cigarettes/day
models.estimates: Relative risk of coronary heart disease at 1, 5 and 20 cigarettes/day vs never smokers, by sex.

valid_for.population: 141 prospective cohorts (55 reports), mostly Europe/N America/East Asia, Medline 1946–May 2015

models.uncertainty: Men's CIs printed; women's CIs are in Table 1 (not rendered in the page I read), shown as null. Across studies the 1-a-day excess was 46% (IQR 24–56%) of the 20-a-day excess in men. Multi-adjusted estimates are higher. Second-hand smoke in the reference group may bias RRs down.

source.citation: Hackshaw A, Morris JK, Boniface S, Tang JL, Milenković D. Low cigarette consumption and risk of coronary heart disease and stroke: meta-analysis of 141 cohort studies in 55 study reports. BMJ 2018;360:j5855
source.where: Results, 'Coronary heart disease'; Abstract; multi-adjusted values from 'Confounding' section
source.quote: The pooled relative risk from 26 study reports was 1.48 (95% confidence interval 1.30 to 1.69) for men who smoked, on average, one cigarette per day and 1.58 (1.39 to 1.80) for those who smoked five cigarettes per day; the relative risk for smoking 20 cigarettes per day was 2.04 (1.86 to 2.24)

supporting_sources.citation: Bjartveit K, Tverdal A. Tob Control 2005;14:315-320
supporting_sources.note: 1–4/day IHD death RR 2.74 (2.07–3.61) men, 2.94 (1.75–4.95) women. Abstract only.

supporting_sources.citation: Banks E et al. BMC Med 2019;17:128
supporting_sources.note: Acute MI: current 2.45 (2.22–2.70); 25+/day 3.34 (2.85–3.92). Useful for >20/day, but a different source.
India, death from heart disease, any smoking: men 1.6 (1.5–1.8), women 1.7 (1.3–2.1), 99% CI. No dose bands.

models.caveats: The curve is steep at low doses then flattens, so cutting down helps the heart much less than people expect. The same paper reports cohorts where heavy smokers who halved their smoking had CVD RR 1.06, 1.02 and 0.92 vs continuing heavy smokers, while quitters had 0.67, 0.46 and 0.43. Between points, log-linear interpolation (ln RR linear in cigs) matches the authors' modelling approach but is our step, not a published coefficient; please confirm. Do not extrapolate above 20/day with this table.
models.user_copy: Heart attack risk: about +{pct}% vs a non-smoker at {n} a day (range {lo}–{hi}%). Even 1 a day carries about half the extra risk of 20 a day.

source.citation: Doll R, Peto R, Boreham J, Sutherland I. BMJ 2004;328:1519

supporting_sources.note: Lung cancer death HR 9.12 (2.92–28.47) for <1/day and 11.61 (8.25–16.35) for 1–10/day (abstract).

models.name: Pack-years and lung cancer screening threshold
models.estimates: Cumulative cigarette exposure in pack-years and whether the user meets the USPSTF 2021 lung cancer screening criteria.

inputs.how_we_get_it: one-time question for past average, plus log

models.formula: pack_years = (avg_cigs_per_day / 20) * years_smoked; eligible = age >= 50 && age <= 80 && pack_years >= 20 && years_since_quit <= 15
models.uncertainty: Guideline threshold, not a risk estimate.

source.citation: US Preventive Services Task Force. Screening for lung cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation statement. JAMA 2021;325(10):962-970; and USPSTF Clinician Summary, March 2021

source.quote: One pack-year is the equivalent of smoking an average of 20 cigarettes—1 pack—per day for a year.

This is a US guideline; I did not find an Indian screening guideline in this pass. Show as 'talk to a doctor about screening', never as a diagnosis.
models.user_copy: Your smoking history is about {pack_years} pack-years. In the US, people aged 50–80 with 20+ pack-years are offered yearly lung scans. Worth a chat with a doctor.

recommend: Show first: (1) smoking-dose-chd and (2) smoking-dose-stroke — they are the per-disease, dose-moving screen you want, from a 141-cohort meta-analysis with CIs, and they carry the key honest message that cutting down helps the heart far less than quitting. (3) smoking-dose-allcause-india plus smoking-life-years-lost-india — Indian, nationally representative, and the 1–7/day row makes 'light smoking isn't safe' concrete. (4) smoking-tb-india — highly relevant to Indian users and rarely known. (5) smoking-life-expectancy-per-cigarette — easy daily-log feedback ('today ≈ N minutes'), labelled as a population average. Lung cancer and COPD tables (Doll) are a good second row because they show the roughly linear cancer curve next to the flat heart curve. Part 2 of H1 should cover the not_found items (other cancers, non-fatal conditions, FEV1, Carter 2015, US SG 2014).
